Volume 09 · Chapter 04

CAPM and equilibrium risk pricing

Advanced Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v09-c03

By the endDerive the CAPM mechanism and distinguish its theoretical assumptions from empirical evidence.

Capability and prerequisites

You can derive the capital asset pricing model (CAPM) from investor choice and market clearing, calculate beta and alpha with a stated benchmark, and distinguish an equilibrium restriction from a regression identity or empirical finding. Use simple total returns and beginning-wealth budgets, covariance and diversification, and mean-variance allocation. The CAPM used conditionally in corporate cost-of-capital estimation now receives its equilibrium argument.

An analyst calls a high-volatility security expensive because its expected return is low. Another finds a positive regression intercept and calls it evidence of skill. Neither conclusion follows from the statistic alone. We must identify which risk investors bear at the margin, why a particular portfolio prices that risk, and what was actually tested. A covariance formula defines beta; investor optimality plus an economy's supply constraints do the economic work.

All numerical returns and investor descriptions below are original synthetic examples. They are not observed market data or investment recommendations. Unless explicitly changed, there is one annual interval, one fictional currency, no fees or taxes, and all final cash includes distributions and liquidation proceeds. Return means are physical expectations, not promises.

1. Define the economy before using the line

There are n risky claims with simple total-return vector R, mean μ = E[R] and covariance matrix Σ. Assume finite second moments and Σ symmetric positive definite (SPD). A risk-free position has certain simple return rf, with 1+rf > 0. Let e = μ−rf1 denote the vector of expected excess returns; 1 is the vector of ones. Every return refers to the same horizon and currency.

Investor h has positive beginning wealth Wh and chooses risky wealth exposures xh. The cash or borrowing weight is ch = 1−1′xh; a negative value means borrowing. Risky exposures may also be negative. All investors can trade divisible claims without costs or taxes and can borrow or lend at the same rf, without quantity limits. They share the same beliefs about μ and Σ and evaluate the same horizon. For the model's empirical restriction, these common moments are also assumed to describe the physical return distribution; agreement alone could otherwise be mistaken. There is no outside nontraded income or unmodeled wealth in this economy.

Assume directly that investor h maximizes the mean-variance criterion

Uh(x) = E[Rp,h] − (γh/2)Var(Rp,h)
= rf + x′e − (γh/2)x′Σx,   γh > 0.

Here γh penalizes return variance; it is not automatically the same coefficient as absolute risk aversion over dollar wealth. We are not proving that every expected-utility investor ranks arbitrary distributions by two moments. Certain preference/distribution restrictions can justify such reductions; outside them, skewness, downside losses or other features may matter. The finite-state case below uses the stated criterion as its behavioral premise.

The market portfolio holds every risky claim in this modeled economy in proportion to its beginning market value. If Pi > 0 and net outstanding units Ni > 0, its weights are wM,i = PiNi/ΣjPjNj. This is a supply-weighted object, not whichever index happens to be convenient. We choose zero aggregate net supply of the risk-free borrowing/lending claims, so aggregate investor wealth W equals total risky market value. This normalization simplifies the proof; zero net risk-free supply is not a universal requirement for every formulation of CAPM.

Sharpe's original 1964 paper connects portfolio choice to equilibrium under common expectations and equal borrowing/lending terms. The explicit quadratic-objective derivation here is our own restricted presentation. Its assumptions and sufficiency claims should be assessed as stated, rather than attributed wholesale to every historical version of the model.

2. From individual first-order conditions to market clearing

Differentiate with respect to each risky exposure. The cash budget is already substituted into the objective, so there is no additional requirement that the risky weights alone sum to one:

∇Uh = e−γhΣxh = 0,
x*h = (1/γh)Σ−1e.

The Hessian is −γhΣ, negative definite. Thus this condition identifies the unique global maximum, not merely a stationary point. Indeed, for any perturbation d around x*h, the objective change is −(γh/2)d′Σd, strictly negative for nonzero d. All investors choose the same risky direction Σ−1e and differ in scale because of risk aversion. The direction need not sum to one for arbitrary candidate prices; that normalization must be justified.

Let ah = Wh/W be each investor's positive wealth share, summing to one. Market clearing requires the wealth-weighted risky demands to equal the outstanding risky market weights:

wM = Σhahx*h = TΣ−1e,
T = Σhah/γh > 0.
Therefore e = λΣwM,   λ = 1/T > 0.

This is the step a beta definition cannot supply. It equates desired ownership with actual supply at equilibrium prices. Because 1′wM = 1, it also gives 1′Σ−1e = 1/T > 0: the positive normalization needed for the tangency fund in Chapter 3 follows in this equilibrium. Aggregate cash demand is Σah(1−1′x*h) = 0, matching its chosen zero net supply.

The ith entry of ΣwM is Cov(Ri, RM). Multiplying the vector equation by w′M gives the market's own premium. SPD and nonzero market weights imply positive market variance:

μi−rf = λCov(Ri,RM),
μM−rf = λVar(RM) > 0.
βi = Cov(Ri,RM)/Var(RM),
μi = rf + βi(μM−rf).

The result prices covariance with aggregate risky wealth. Increasing a small exposure to claim i changes the variance of the market position at rate 2Cov(Ri,RM); the factor of two cancels the one-half in the variance penalty. A claim that pays relatively well when the market is weak can have negative covariance and a required return below rf. Its expected premium compensates for its contribution to portfolio risk, rather than its stand-alone variance.

This is a conditional equilibrium derivation. It does not prove existence or uniqueness of prices for every possible endowment/payoff economy, nor a global price-adjustment process. Changing expected payoffs at fixed prices generally breaks clearing: prices, return moments, wealth shares or other equilibrium quantities would then have to adjust. The next case exhibits a consistent equilibrium directly.

Worked example 1 — Caldera's investors clear every claim

Caldera Market has three claims A, B and C, each priced at 100 CU. Outstanding units are 3, 2 and 1, so total market value is 600 and wM = (1/2, 1/3, 1/6). Four states each have physical probability 1/4. The risk-free return is 2%.

s298 / −2%101 / 1%80 / −20%−4%

Physical means are μ = (0.08, 0.06, 0). The market mean is 0.06 and its deviations are (−0.10, −0.10, 0.10, 0.10), giving variance 0.01. Direct centered state products give:

Σ = [[1/40, 3/200, −3/200],
     [3/200, 1/80, −1/100],
     [−3/200, −1/100, 7/200]].

For instance Cov(A,B) = [0.030+0.005+0.015+0.010]/4 = 0.015. The leading principal minors are 1/40, 7/80000 and 9/4000000, all positive, establishing SPD for this symmetric matrix. ΣwM = (0.015, 0.010, −0.005). Thus betas are (1.5, 1, −0.5) and the CAPM with market premium 4% gives expected returns (8%, 6%, 0%), exactly the physical means.

Do preferences actually support those prices? Investor H1 has wealth 200 and γ = 2; H2 has wealth 400 and γ = 8. T = (1/3)/2 + (2/3)/8 = 1/4, so λ = 4. Also Σ−1e = (2, 4/3, 2/3) = 4wM. The individually optimal holdings are:

H1 borrows 200 from H2 and owes 204 at date 1. H1 owns twice the market exposure and has state returns (−10%, −10%, 30%, 30%); H2 owns half the market exposure and has (−1%, −1%, 9%, 9%). Their final wealth sums to (576, 576, 696, 696), exactly the risky economy's total final cash. The loan cancels across investors. Individual optimality, risky supplies, funding and state cash all reconcile; matching a line in a scatterplot alone would not establish this.

3. The security market line and capital market line answer different questions

The security market line (SML) plots expected return against beta. Under this CAPM, every claim and every fixed-weight portfolio, including inefficient portfolios, satisfies it. For beginning risky weights w and cash weight 1−1′w, covariance linearity gives βp = Σwiβi. Cash has beta zero, and βM = 1. These relations hold with signed weights and do not require independent residual risks.

The capital market line (CML) is the efficient upper boundary in expected-return versus total standard deviation space when the market is the tangency portfolio. Its upper ray consists of nonnegative market exposure y and cash weight 1−y:

Rp = rf + y(RM−rf),
μp = rf + y(μM−rf),   σp = |y|σM.
For y ≥ 0: μp = rf + [(μM−rf)/σM]σp.

Why is this the upper boundary? For any risky exposure x, the equilibrium relation gives μp−rf = λx′ΣwM. Cauchy–Schwarz in the Σ inner product bounds this by λ√(x′Σx)√(w′MΣwM) = σp(μM−rf)/σM. With SPD, equality on the upper ray requires x to be a nonnegative multiple of wM. A negative y instead puts the portfolio on the lower ray; it does not become efficient by replacing y with |y| in the expected-return formula.

Keep each horizontal axis and claim set explicit
RelationRisk coordinateWhat lies on it in this model?
SMLBeta, a covariance exposureEvery correctly priced claim and fixed-weight portfolio
Upper CMLTotal return standard deviationEfficient nonnegative market/cash combinations
Return projectionRealized benchmark excess returnA fitted linear relation with a residual; it is not itself either pricing line

Define the population projection on market excess return:

Ri−rf = αi + βi(RM−rf) + εi,
βi = Cov(Ri,RM)/Var(RM),
αi = μi−rf−βi(μM−rf).

Choosing the least-squares intercept and slope ensures E[εi] = 0 and Cov(εi,RM) = 0; these are projection identities. The CAPM adds the economic restriction αi = 0. Orthogonality is not independence or causation. Variance decomposes as β²iσ²M + Var(εi), so residual risk can be large even when its mean premium is zero. At fixed portfolio weights, alpha also combines linearly, including a zero alpha for cash.

Worked example 2 — A zero-beta risky portfolio and an inefficient security

In Caldera, C has total variance 7/200 = 0.035, greater than A's 1/40 = 0.025, yet C's beta is −0.5 and its expected return is 0%, below the 2% risk-free return. Its market component has variance (−0.5)²×0.01 = 0.0025; residual variance is 0.0325. C pays 30% in one bad-market state and −20% in the other. Negative beta is an average covariance statement, not a guarantee of protection in every bad state.

Now hold one-quarter A and three-quarters C. Its beta is 0.25×1.5+0.75×(−0.5) = 0; mean return is 0.25×8% = 2%. Its four returns are (19.5%, −15.5%, 4.5%, −0.5%). Centering around 2% gives (17.5%, −17.5%, 2.5%, −2.5%), with variance 1/64 and standard deviation 12.5%. It lies at beta zero on the SML but is not risk-free or on the upper CML. Cash delivers the same mean with zero variance.

A alone has mean 8% and standard deviation √0.025 ≈ 15.8114%. A portfolio with y = 1.5 in the market and −0.5 in cash also has mean 2%+1.5×4% = 8%, but variance 1.5²×0.01 = 0.0225 and standard deviation 15%. It dominates A in the mean-variance ranking, although A is correctly priced and has zero CAPM alpha. The return difference contains residual risk; it is not a guaranteed arbitrage profit in every state.

4. Physical expectations are not pricing probabilities

The physical probabilities describe how frequently states are expected to occur. They determine μ, Σ and beta in the preceding economy. An expected payoff divided by 1+rf is generally not its price when the payoff is risky. The CAPM instead relates physical expected returns to their covariance risk. Equivalently, a consistent contingent-payoff pricing rule can assign different valuation weights to states, reflecting the value of cash in those states.

Worked example 3 — One physical distribution, different valuation weights

Keep Caldera's physical probabilities (1/4,1/4,1/4,1/4). A's physical expected payoff is 108, B's is 106 and C's is 100. Discounting all at 2% would give approximately 105.882353, 103.921569 and 98.039216, inconsistent with their equilibrium prices of 100. Their distinct CAPM required returns instead give 108/1.08 = 106/1.06 = 100/1 = 100.

For a finite-state consistency check, construct the separate normalized valuation weights q = (7/20, 7/20, 3/20, 3/20). All are positive and sum to one. Under q, each claim's expected payoff is 102; for A, 0.35×88+0.35×98+0.15×118+0.15×128 = 102. Thus Eq[payoff]/1.02 = 100 for every claim. The high weights are attached to the two low-market states, although their physical probabilities remain 1/4.

These weights can be checked directly from ms = [1−4(RM,s−0.06)]/1.02 and qs = psms(1.02). Here m = (70/51,70/51,10/17,10/17) is strictly positive, prices the risk-free payoff and satisfies ΣpsmsXi,s = Pi for all three claims. This verifies an economically consistent price rule for the constructed economy. Arbitrary mean-variance data need not make this linear candidate positive or satisfy every claim identity. General discount-factor theory and completeness are developed in the planned next chapter.

Never substitute q for p when estimating the physical expected return or covariance because it makes the pricing arithmetic convenient. Nor does the four-state construction estimate real investors' beliefs. Physical probabilities, state valuation weights and required expected returns are distinct objects connected here by explicitly checked identities.

5. Alpha can change when the benchmark or sample changes

For a chosen benchmark P, the population excess-return projection has slope βiP and intercept αiP. It is always possible to define that projection when Var(RP) > 0 and second moments exist. It does not follow that P is the equilibrium market. If all population alphas in a tested asset universe are zero and P has a positive excess mean, then e = [(μP−rf)/σ²P]ΣwP: the same algebra identifies P as a tangency portfolio within that opportunity set. This does not establish that all economically relevant wealth has been included.

A finite sample replaces expectations by averages. With constant rf, write Xt = RP,t−rf and Yt = Ri,t−rf. Ordinary least squares gives

β̂ = Σt(Xt−X̄)(Yt−Ȳ) / Σt(Xt−X̄)²,
α̂ = Ȳ−β̂X̄.

The common covariance/variance divisor cancels. A sample slope is an estimate, not the true beta by definition. An estimated intercept can differ from zero through sample noise, benchmark choice, changing exposures, model failure or data construction. With a time-varying risk-free rate, first construct matching excess returns for every date; subtracting one average rate after an inconsistent regression does not generally reproduce that specification. Any statistical test needs its sampling assumptions and an appropriate uncertainty calculation.

Worked example 4 — Apparent alpha with no failure of the true-market CAPM

Use Caldera's complete population but incorrectly label B alone as the market proxy. Its variance is 1/80 = 0.0125 and excess mean is 4%. Covariances with B are (0.015,0.0125,−0.01), giving proxy betas (1.2,1,−0.8). Therefore:

αA,B = 0.08−0.02−1.2(0.06−0.02) = 0.012,
αB,B = 0,
αC,B = 0−0.02−(−0.8)(0.06−0.02) = 0.012.

A and C appear to have 1.2 percentage points of alpha, although all true-market alphas are exactly zero. B's alpha against itself is automatically zero and supplies no independent evidence of correct pricing. Relative to B, the actual market has beta 0.8 and alpha 0.008. The wrong proxy is inefficient; the finding is not proof of exploitable security mispricing or manager skill.

Now use the true market but observe only this selected eight-state sequence: s1, s2, s3, s4, s1, s3, s3, s4. This is an allowed pedagogical sample, not observed history or a random simulation. A's sample mean is 10.5% and the market's is 8.5%, rather than population 8% and 6%. The centered market sum of squares is 3/40, and its centered cross-product with A is 23/200. Thus β̂A = 23/15; α̂A = 0.085−(23/15)×0.065 = −11/750 ≈ −1.466667%. The true population beta remains 1.5 and alpha remains zero. The sign or size of this one sample intercept is not an empirical refutation, a significance test or a forecast of persistence.

6. What an empirical test can and cannot identify

A CAPM pricing restriction concerns expectations at equilibrium. A regression uses realized observations and a measurable proxy. A credible empirical design therefore needs a specified asset universe, return convention, benchmark, information set, period, costs and sampling model. A cross-section of noisy estimated betas adds an errors-in-variables problem; multiple asset residuals can also be correlated. Estimating a slope or reporting a high R² does not resolve either problem.

Fama and French's 2004 paper discusses zero-intercept and cross-sectional tests, the elusive comprehensive market portfolio, and the limits of interpreting proxy-based rejections. Their historical assessment is evidence about the studies and period they discuss, not an October 2026 result. Our counterexample shows why a proxy rejection need not refute the true-market relation. That logical possibility does not validate arbitrary applications: using a proxy to set required returns needs its own defense.

The joint-hypothesis problem arises when a pricing-model residual is used to judge whether prices correctly reflect information. The conclusion jointly maintains the expected-return model, the chosen market proxy and relevant data/statistical assumptions. A rejection of their conjunction does not identify which part failed. A nonrejection does not prove the conjunction true: the test may have low power, omitted assets or a short sample. The synthetic Caldera proxy example isolates one failure mechanism; it does not claim that actual empirical anomalies are all proxy errors.

There are at least three different claims to audit. Theoretical: common beliefs, feasible trading and mean-variance choice imply a particular relation. Statistical: a specified data-generating process and sample support or reject a coefficient restriction with stated uncertainty. Investment: an implementable policy can earn an attractive net outcome after costs, financing and risks. Passing one audit does not automatically pass the others. A positive estimated alpha may disappear after fees, selection correction, a changed benchmark or a fresh sample; a significant residual would still require an economic explanation.

An empirical investigation should record total returns including relevant distributions, common currency and matched dates, survivorship and delisting treatment, an ex-ante universe and benchmark, funding costs, model specification and exposure stability. It should separate model selection from evaluation and account for the search across many candidate strategies. Those are research-design requirements, not claims that any particular historical premium exists today. Detailed factor estimation and inference continue in planned Chapter 6.

7. Find the exact assumption that changes the proof

Constraints and funding spreads. If investor h cannot borrow, then 1′xh ≤ 1. With unrestricted risky short sales otherwise, a binding constraint contributes a multiplier ηh ≥ 0:

e−γhΣxh = ηh1,
ηh(1′xh−1) = 0.

The risky direction can now depend on both γ and the individual constraint. Simply scaling the original common fund down is not generally optimal. Different borrowing/lending rates similarly make the cash part of the objective piecewise rather than one common linear term. One cannot reuse the unrestricted first-order condition unchanged and announce that the original equilibrium still clears.

Different beliefs. Investor-specific μh or Σh prevent factoring the same Σ−1e out of aggregate demand. A more general equilibrium may exist, but the displayed proof no longer establishes its CAPM. Singular covariance. Redundant claims can make Σ only positive semidefinite. Our inverse and unique-demand claims then do not apply without reducing the independent payoff span or checking additional conditions. If market variance is zero, its beta denominator is undefined.

Nontraded income. To see the mechanism rather than simply listing an omission, give investor h a random outside income return Yh, measured per unit of the same financial beginning wealth. Let kh = Cov(R,Yh). Total variance includes x′Σx + 2x′kh + Var(Yh), so the first-order condition becomes e = γh(Σxh+kh). Under the same financial-supply accounting, aggregation yields

e = (1/T)[ΣwM + Σhahkh].

Covariance with the financial market alone need not summarize the extra exposure. This is a deliberately limited extension, not a complete human-capital pricing theorem. Calling an equity index “total wealth” neither measures nontraded income nor makes it tradable. The no-outside-income assumption in the original proof is substantive.

Dynamic and higher-moment risks. A one-period constant-parameter restriction cannot automatically price changing investment opportunities, consumption needs or nonlinear downside preferences over many dates. These limitations identify where the derivation must change; they do not make covariance irrelevant. The model remains useful as a transparent benchmark when its perimeter and uncertainty are stated.

8. Reproduce the equilibrium and make it fail honestly

Save the synthetic inputs, complete Python benchmark, exact reference output, file manifest and execution and model guide together. Run python3 v09-c04-analysis.py, optionally supplying a different input path. It uses standard-library fractions, imports quietly, writes no files and needs no network. Variances remain exact rather than rounding their square roots. A coefficient such as -11/750 is a decimal return, approximately −1.466667%, not −0.014667%.

Independently reconstruct one covariance entry, each investor's budget and the aggregate units before comparing output. Then inspect two interventions. First, add one percentage point to every state return of A while holding prices and supplies fixed: the code reports excess demand rather than inventing a new equilibrium. Second, prohibit only H1 from borrowing and verify the constrained optimum and failed clearing. Asset and investor selectors are used explicitly; an unsupported funding-regime label is rejected. Edited candidate economies may return market_clearing=false or fail the pricing-checksum flag. That is a finding, not a reason to change physical probabilities until the answer passes.

The selected sample's reported residual variance uses divisor n as an empirical mean square. It is not an alpha standard error or the residual variance estimator with divisor n−2. The benchmark calculates no significance level or real-world performance claim. Independent numerical checks assess this bounded case; they do not validate actual market efficiency.

Practice

  1. In a separate economy satisfying the theorem's assumptions, three investors have wealth shares (1/5,3/10,1/2) and return-risk-aversion coefficients (2,3,5). Derive aggregate T and λ from individual first-order conditions. If market variance is 0.018 and rf = 1%, find the market expected return, the required return of a claim with beta −1/4, and each investor's market and cash exposure. Verify aggregate cash clearing. Explain why the negative-beta claim's expected return need not be positive.
  2. Using Caldera, form the fully invested portfolio D with weights 4 in A, −6 in the true market and 3 in cash. Calculate all four returns, its mean, variance and beta. Relate it to the residual part of A and explain whether a 20% standard deviation requires a positive expected excess return in this equilibrium. State the trading permission needed to implement D.
  3. In a separate one-year conditional CAPM exercise, rf = 3%, μM = 9% and σM = 20%. A security has beta 0.5, expected return 7% and standard deviation 30%. Compute its CAPM alpha. Find the market/cash combination with the same 30% standard deviation on the conditional CAPM benchmark line and its expected return. Distinguish that benchmark from the true efficient frontier once the supplied positive-alpha security is admitted. For a portfolio holding 60% of the security and 40% cash, compute mean, beta and alpha. Does a positive alpha mean that the security lies on the CML or creates a guaranteed arbitrage?
  4. Use Caldera's positive valuation weights from worked example 3 to price a zero-net-supply contract paying 1 CU only in s1 and zero otherwise. Calculate its physical expected return, covariance with the market, beta and CAPM required return. Compare its price with discounting the physical expected payoff at 2%. Explain how its expected return can be negative without a pricing inconsistency. You may use the supplied finite-state pricing rule; no general completeness theorem is required.
  5. For the eight observations s1,s2,s3,s4,s1,s3,s3,s4, use A and the true Caldera market. Reconstruct both sample means, the centered market sum of squares, the centered cross-product, OLS beta and excess-return alpha. Explain why dividing both covariance sums by n−1 leaves beta unchanged. Does the intercept by itself refute the known population CAPM or supply an alpha standard error?
  6. Instead use the equal-weighted Caldera risky portfolio E = (A+B+C)/3 as the proxy. Compute its mean and variance, all three proxy betas and alphas, and the equally weighted average alpha. Compare C's alpha with the B-only result. Explain why a proxy's zero alpha against itself does not identify the true market. Use the displayed covariance matrix rather than treating equal weights as market-value weights.
  7. Keep Caldera's original prices and beliefs but forbid H1 from borrowing; risky short sales remain unrestricted. Show that xH1 = (1,0,0), cash zero, satisfies the constrained first-order conditions with η = 0.01 and is the unique optimum. Compare H1's objective there with holding the unleveraged market. Keep H2 unchanged and calculate aggregate risky exposures, excess demands and cash demand. Do the old prices still clear? Explain why merely clipping the original cash weight or scaling H1 down to one market unit is insufficient.
  8. A hypothetical monthly study selects the best of 100 strategies on the same 24 observations. It reports gross alpha 0.8% per month against a domestic stock index and a standard error of 0.5%, then claims “CAPM is disproved, prices are irrational and persistent skill is proven.” A deterministic fee of 0.3% of beginning wealth is charged each month; it has no return covariance. Calculate gross and net approximate intervals using the supplied normal-reference multiplier 1.96, while stating that its validity has not been established for this selected sample. Write a research-audit response addressing the joint hypothesis, market coverage, nontraded wealth, sampling/selection, implementation and an independent evaluation design.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. The individual first-order condition gives xh = Σ−1e/γh. Aggregating gives T = (1/5)/2 + (3/10)/3 + (1/2)/5 = 3/10 and λ = 10/3. Market premium is (10/3)×0.018 = 6%, so μM = 7%. The claim's required return is 1%−(1/4)×6% = −0.5%. The market exposures λ/γ are (5/3,10/9,2/3); cash exposures are (−2/3,−1/9,1/3). Weighted cash is −2/15−1/30+1/6 = 0, while weighted market exposure is one. Negative covariance can make a claim valuable for risk reduction even with an expected loss. This is an expected-return statement under the model, not a guaranteed payment or permission to discard the claim's state risks.

  2. The weights sum to 4−6+3 = 1, including cash. D's return is 4RA−6RM+3×0.02, giving (−18%,22%,−18%,22%). Its mean is 2%, deviations are (−20%,20%,−20%,20%), variance is 0.04 and standard deviation 20%. Beta is 4×1.5−6×1 = 0. A's market-projection residuals are (−5%,5%,−5%,5%), so RD = 2%+4εA. Residual mean and market covariance are zero, leaving no CAPM excess mean despite the substantial variance. Implementation needs the stipulated ability to short six units of market exposure and hold the resulting cash, with no omitted shorting fee or restriction. It is not an ordinary long-only diversified fund.

  3. The security's CAPM required return is 3%+0.5×6% = 6%, so alpha is 1%. On the conditional CAPM market/cash benchmark line, y = 30%/20% = 1.5, cash weight is −0.5, and expected return is 3%+1.5×6% = 12%. This is a valid market/cash combination. It cannot be called the actual efficient frontier after admitting the supplied positive-alpha security: the zero-alpha condition used to establish market tangency has failed, and the additional residual exposure can improve the opportunity set under unrestricted trading. The security itself has more total risk than its beta alone measures and does not lie on the displayed benchmark line.

    The 60/40 portfolio has mean 0.6×7%+0.4×3% = 5.4%, beta 0.6×0.5 = 0.3, required return 4.8% and alpha 0.6%. Its positive alpha is a conditional expected-return departure from the CAPM; it does not eliminate residual risk or create a guaranteed state-by-state profit. The stated security mean is inconsistent with an exact zero-alpha CAPM equilibrium, so it must be interpreted as a proposed departure, estimate or model failure.

  4. The contract price is (7/20)/1.02 = 35/102 CU. Its physical expected payoff is 1/4, so expected return is (1/4)/(35/102)−1 = −19/70 ≈ −27.142857%. Since the claim pays only in s1, Cov(RD,RM) = [(1/4)/(35/102)](−0.04−0.06) = −51/700. Divide by market variance 1/100 to get beta −51/7. CAPM gives 1/50+(−51/7)(1/25) = −19/70, matching the physical expected return. Physical-mean discounting would give (1/4)/1.02 = 25/102, below the correct 35/102. The payoff is concentrated in a heavily valued bad-market state; the buyer accepts a negative mean return for that exposure. In the other states the return is −100%, so this is not a certain hedge. Zero net supply leaves the original aggregate market payoff unchanged.

  5. A's observed returns sum to 0.84, giving mean 0.105. The market has three returns of −0.04 and five of 0.16, summing to 0.68 and averaging 0.085. Centered market values are −0.125 three times and 0.075 five times, so the sum of squares is 3×0.125²+5×0.075² = 3/40. Multiplying centered A and market observations and summing gives 23/200. Beta is (23/200)/(3/40) = 23/15. Excess-return means are 0.085 for A and 0.065 for the market, so alpha is 0.085−(23/15)×0.065 = −11/750. Dividing numerator and denominator by seven cancels in beta. This finite sample is compatible with the supplied population relation; its frequencies differ from the physical probabilities. A point estimate alone neither refutes the relation nor gives an uncertainty estimate. The lab's sample residual mean square uses divisor eight and is not an alpha standard error.

  6. μE = (0.08+0.06+0)/3 = 7/150. The covariance vector Σ(1/3,1/3,1/3)′ is (1/120,7/1200,1/300), so σ²E = 7/1200. Betas are (10/7,1,4/7); the proxy excess mean is 7/150−1/50 = 2/75. Alphas are 3/50−(10/7)(2/75) = 23/1050 for A; 1/25−2/75 = 1/75 for B; and −1/50−(4/7)(2/75) = −37/1050 for C. Their equally weighted average is zero because 23+14−37 = 0. C changes from +1.2% against B to approximately −3.523810% against E, while its true-market alpha remains zero. A proxy has beta one and alpha zero relative to itself by construction. Such self-comparison cannot establish that the proxy includes the true supply-weighted market or is efficient against other available assets.

  7. For H1, e = (0.06,0.04,−0.02). At x = (1,0,0), e−2Σx = (0.06−0.05,0.04−0.03,−0.02+0.03) = (0.01,0.01,0.01). Thus η = 0.01 ≥ 0, the budget binds with 1′x = 1, and complementary slackness holds. For any other feasible z, concavity gives U(z)−U(x) = η1′(z−x)−(2/2)(z−x)′Σ(z−x) ≤ 0, strictly negative for z≠x. This proves unique global optimality. U(A) = 0.08−0.025 = 0.055, versus U(M) = 0.06−0.01 = 0.050.

    H2 still holds (1/4,1/6,1/12) and cash 1/2. Wealth-weighted risky demand is (1/3)(1,0,0)+(2/3)(1/4,1/6,1/12) = (1/2,1/9,1/18). Subtract supplies (1/2,1/3,1/6): excess demand is (0,−2/9,−1/9). Net cash demand is (2/3)(1/2) = 1/3, or 200 CU, despite zero net cash supply. The old prices do not clear. Clipping cash to zero while leaving old risky weights unchanged violates the wealth budget; scaling to one market unit respects the budget but fails individual optimality. A new constrained equilibrium needs a new price analysis.

  8. The nominal gross interval is 0.8%±1.96×0.5% = [−0.18%,1.78%] per month. The deterministic fee subtracts 0.3 percentage points from every return, leaving beta and the stated standard error unchanged under this simplified treatment. Net alpha is 0.5% and its same-reference interval is [−0.48%,1.48%]. Even these unadjusted intervals include zero. They are calculations under the supplied multiplier, not validated confidence statements for the selected study.

    A strong audit distinguishes the joint pricing/proxy hypothesis from a direct test of investor rationality. It asks whether the domestic index covers relevant traded wealth and whether outside labor/property exposures invalidate the assumed investor problem. It checks common total-return dates, funding and fee treatment, survivorship/delisting information, time variation and residual dependence. Selecting the best of 100 strategies on the same short sample changes inference; the reported standard error alone does not correct selection. Require a prespecified universe, strategy and benchmark, an untouched or genuinely prospective evaluation period, a disclosed search history, suitable uncertainty methods and implementable trading/financing costs. Alternative model/proxy explanations and sample noise remain possible. Neither persistent skill, a general CAPM rejection nor irrational prices is established by this report. Grade the separation of hypotheses and concrete design repairs, rather than demanding one preferred factor model.

Teach-back and delayed check

Teach-back. Explain to a colleague, without starting from the SML formula, why covariance enters the expected return and why the market portfolio is special. Then use Caldera to show that zero alpha does not mean an asset is efficient on its own.

Teach-back benchmark

The variance gradient of a risky position is proportional to its covariance with the investor's portfolio. Common opportunities and unconstrained mean-variance choice produce demands proportional to Σ−1e. Aggregating these optimal demands and equating them to outstanding market-value supplies identifies the market as that common risky fund. This gives e = λΣwM; the market's own equation converts λ into its expected premium divided by variance. A has zero true-market alpha but variance 0.025; a 1.5 market exposure has the same 8% expected return and lower variance 0.0225. Price consistency and stand-alone portfolio efficiency are different claims.

Delayed check. After a week, reconstruct: (i) why the wealth weights matter in aggregation; (ii) the expected return of a zero-beta risky portfolio; (iii) the failure caused by substituting B for the true Caldera market; and (iv) which first-order-condition term appears when borrowing is prohibited.

Delayed-check answer

Investors demand currency amounts Whxh, so aggregate exposures use Wh/W, not an unweighted average of individual portfolios. Under the stated CAPM, a zero-beta portfolio has expected return rf but may retain positive residual variance, as Caldera's one-quarter A/three-quarters C does. Using B creates apparent alphas of 1.2% for A and C despite zero alphas relative to the true market. A binding borrowing constraint contributes ηh1 to e−γhΣxh, with η≥0 and complementary slackness; the common unconstrained risky direction need not survive. These are model deductions, not evidence that a measured future premium is known.

Sources and extension

The sources are the inspected equilibrium sections of Sharpe (1964), the already verified scope of Lo's MIT CAPM lecture, and the scoped discussion of testing and market proxies in Fama and French (2004). These are dated theoretical, teaching and research materials. All Caldera data, demonstrations, proofs as presented, exercises and code are original. Source inspection does not endorse every statement in a paper; in particular, this chapter never treats zero covariance as general independence.

The planned state-price and discount-factor chapter develops contingent-payoff pricing beyond this checksum, while planned factor-model work broadens empirical restrictions and estimation. The CAPM provides a precise benchmark linking choice, aggregate supply and covariance. Using it responsibly requires preserving those distinctions when moving from a theorem to data or a decision.

Sources and further study

  • Andrew W. Lo, MIT 15.401 Finance Theory I — Lectures 15–17: The CAPM and APT (Fall 2008) — Primary teaching reference for covariance risk, CAPM required returns, market-proxy estimation and the distinction between model implications and empirical evidence. Scope: slides 3–9,17–27; no historical example or empirical estimate is imported into the fictional lab.
  • William F. Sharpe — Capital Asset Prices: A Theory of Market Equilibrium under Conditions of Risk (1964) — Original equilibrium argument connecting portfolio choice, common expectations, equal borrowing/lending terms and systematic covariance risk. The chapter supplies its own explicit SPD quadratic-objective proof and original clearing economy.
  • Eugene F. Fama and Kenneth R. French — The Capital Asset Pricing Model: Theory and Evidence (2004) — Primary author paper on the market portfolio/proxy problem, regression pricing restrictions, hypothesis interpretation and implementation limits. The chapter treats the paper's empirical assessment as dated 2004, not current market evidence.
